pages.title: Wari: cities, households and the Moquegua enclave
pages.intro: Compare planned places and local observations in the Moquegua enclave. Separate building phases, household histories, exchange and evidence that remains unplaced.

paragraphs.text: Wari-associated expansion in Moquegua involved building and maintaining an agricultural landscape alongside its hilltop complexes. Nash describes a canal longer than 20 kilometers that brought at least 700 hectares into cultivation, with part operating by around AD 650. Cerro Baúl and nearby Cerro Mejía were settled before 700. Water management, farming and households were therefore central to the enclave. These statements do not date the entire canal to one year or prove that all inhabitants arrived together. The exact canal route was not independently checked. The summit and neighboring settlement have related but distinct archaeological sequences, and their buildings cannot all inherit one common foundation date.
650 is an approximate by-then operating statement for part of the irrigation system.

sections.heading: Households with different ways of living

paragraphs.text: Households in the Moquegua enclave differed in their architecture, diets and ways of preparing food. Nash interprets this diversity as evidence for a polyethnic colonial community, while the birthplace, language and reasons for moving of individual residents remain unresolved. Water access, cooking, storage and work were integral to the enclave’s operation alongside monumental architecture. The approximately 650 orientation shared with irrigation evidence is not a census date: the household comparison concerns the wider archaeological phase. Cerro Baúl and Cerro Mejía also remain distinct places. A broad reference for the colony area does not place a specific Mejía house on the summit or imply a uniform planned neighborhood.
Shares the approximately 650 irrigation orientation. Household diversity summarizes the wider enclave phase; it is not a census or a claim that each household existed in 650.

Moseley and colleagues describe major reorganization around AD 800, when earlier Cerro Baúl summit structures were leveled or replaced. The later complex brought ceremonial buildings, residences and productive areas into a changed arrangement. D-shaped temples and a pottery workshop with raw materials and tools document different activities. A Nazca-style drum in a ceremonial context provides an object connection, without establishing the language or ethnicity of everyone present. This was rebuilding of an existing colony, rather than evidence of a single master plan completed in one year. The approximate phase does not directly date every wall or demonstrate that nearby settlements followed the same schedule.
Approximate contextual rebuilding phase; no precise common foundation for every component.

sections.heading: Work in the brewery and later hillside homes

paragraphs.text: Milling, boiling and fermentation took place in distinct areas of Cerro Baúl’s brewery. Seven boiling firepits and molle remains support a specific account of preparation, while serving vessels and feasting evidence connect that work to gatherings. Nearby Cerro Mejía has later household evidence than the older early-only model allowed. A burnt-seed sample from a late Unit 17 context has a reported calibrated component at AD 882–995, representing 90.2 percent probability. These are different observations: the summit brewery’s contextual phase is not the same measurement as the hillside household’s seed sample. Together they reveal varied productive and domestic activity across the enclave.
900 is a shared orientation point; brewery phase and Mejía calibrated seed range have distinct semantics.

sections.heading: Closing a brewery, not erasing a region

paragraphs.text: Burning in the brewery and the breaking of serving vessels underpin an interpretation of ceremonial closure around AD 1000. The sequence does not establish a battle, identify an attacking army or show that every Wari-associated household left Moquegua simultaneously. The approximate date also comes from an older chronological synthesis. Later research emphasizes varied local histories, including later Cerro Mejía household samples and an unfinished project at Cerro Petroglifo. The brewery’s termination is therefore one building’s history within a wider changing region. Other communities and activities cannot be assigned the same ending simply because they participated in the Wari-associated enclave.
Approximate closure interpretation in older synthesis, not an exact radiocarbon year.

pages.title: Moche: Huacas de Moche and a long-lived urban landscape
pages.intro: Follow particular north-coast communities and construction contexts, rather than assigning every place to one uniform Moche state or one shared ending.

paragraphs.text: Huacas de Moche has a history longer than the monumental Moche phases that make the place famous. Rengifo and colleagues identify early settlement evidence on Cerro Blanco, including components designated PCB 1 and PCB 2 and stone-built rectilinear spaces. Their synthesis places Salinar within a broad regional phase of about 400 BCE to AD 50. That range describes an archaeological tradition and context, not the continuous life of one excavated house. The same study distinguishes the absence of diagnostic Gallinazo negative-painted pottery at Huacas proper from Gallinazo evidence at nearby Huaca Las Estrellas. Early inhabitants therefore belong in the story, with differences between neighboring places preserved rather than folded into an uninterrupted generic occupation.
400 BCE is a broad phase anchor; integer -399 uses astronomical numbering.

sections.heading: Marine foods in an urban household compound

paragraphs.text: Architectural Compound 9 connects the city to daily preparation, storage and eating. The studied complex covered about 656 square meters and contained 48 spaces with residential, kitchen, storage and burial functions. Roselló and colleagues assigned its sampled contexts to AD 470–600 using the chronology available in 2001. Donax clams and hake dominate the marine assemblage, alongside many less common taxa. Those remains show that coastal resources reached an urban community, while the authors’ proposals about selection and redistribution remain interpretations of the pattern. The dates here are the study’s contextual chronology, not newly calibrated measurements; the original radiocarbon BP ages must not be converted to calendar years by simple subtraction.
470 anchors the 2001 study’s 470–600 contextual interval; no new calibration was performed.

sections.heading: A new temple and a changing urban sequence

paragraphs.text: The site synthesis distinguishes the Old Temple from a New Temple phase placed around AD 700–850. This was a landscape repeatedly transformed: superposed urban floors and contexts of craft and food preparation record changes beyond the monumental façades. A recent textile study summarizes the Old Temple’s cessation closer to 650, illustrating why one exact rebuilding date would be misleading. Both sources point to architectural change, but their broad summaries and chronological purposes differ. Later residential contraction around 850 also does not mean every activity stopped. The synthesis identifies subsequent funerary and ritual reuse, including architectural compounds 45 and 47 and parts of Huaca del Sol, preserving the distinction between a changed city and an empty site.
700 anchors the synthesis’s 700–850 phase; alternative transition around 650 remains explicit.

sections.heading: Textiles extend the history of Moche practice

paragraphs.text: Textiles from Huaca del Sol’s Section 4 reveal a later history than older narratives of abrupt Moche disappearance allowed. Twenty AMS measurements on selected pieces from an assemblage of more than 200 fragments concentrate in the tenth century, with some distributions extending across AD 1000. Techniques and imagery include locally S-spun cotton Moche forms, Highland Moche combinations, Moche-Wari forms and Wari material. These are useful categories for practices and objects, not direct labels for each person’s ethnicity or language. Dates measure fibre growth rather than death or burial; reopened tombs and possible heirlooms complicate deposition. The evidence nevertheless supports continued, changing traditions in a place whose major urban and temple phases had already shifted.
950 anchors the tenth-century concentration; individual calibrated ranges and burial histories differ.

sections.heading: Chimú families use the older sacred landscape

paragraphs.text: Later cemetery evidence shows that the significance of Huacas de Moche did not end with the contraction of its Moche-period city. Rengifo and colleagues assign an Early Chimú group of 25 individuals to approximately AD 1100–1250, supported by two radiocarbon determinations. This does not date every person to the same moment, but it establishes another phase of funerary use in the inherited landscape. The authors distinguish a subsequent Middle Chimú group of eighteen burials, dated relatively rather than by radiocarbon. Keeping those methods separate matters: an archaeological phase can organize the narrative without creating laboratory precision that the evidence does not have. The continuity is one of place and practice, not proof that political institutions or personal identities remained unchanged.
1150 is a contextual anchor within the 1100–1250 phase supported by two dates.

sections.heading: Late Chimú activity in an enduring place

paragraphs.text: A hearth in Architectural Compound 43 supplies a specific late Chimú observation within this long-lived landscape. The published charcoal determination has a calibrated component of AD 1390–1451 representing 90.2 percent probability; it is not the complete 95.4 percent distribution, nor a direct date for every activity in the compound. The broader site synthesis also describes late offerings involving miniature objects, Spondylus and feathered garments, followed by evidence associated with the Chimú-Inca period. These different contexts show continued use but must not be merged into one ceremony. Nearby Huanchaquito-Las Llamas is a separate archaeological locality, and no evidence here makes its mass killing an event inside Compound 43 or identifies the hearth’s particular users.
1420 anchors a reported 1390–1451 calibrated component; probability and charcoal-context caveats remain explicit.

pages.title: Teotihuacan
pages.intro: Look inside the city’s building sequence, changing apartment compounds and later tunnel occupations. Different neighbourhoods did not share one simple ending.

paragraphs.text: The Sun Pyramid presents a long building history behind its apparently unified mass. Excavators distinguish the earlier landscape, construction of the main pyramid, and the adjoining adosada platform. An artificial tunnel adds another architectural layer below the monument. Sugiyama and colleagues proposed a main-building date of 170–310 CE and a tunnel date of 140–240 CE; Sload argues for an earlier chronology. The scene therefore introduces a growing monumental center while showing how excavated sequences can support competing construction histories.
Viewing year within disputed construction model, not completion year.

La Ventilla brings the view away from the pyramids and into a neighborhood of compounds. Archaeologists distinguish an elite and administrative compound, LV 2, from LV 3, associated with lapidary workers. These settings make households, specialized production and unequal access to space part of the city's history. The later dating study also shows why a ceramic label is not a direct label for a political regime. At this viewing year the existing city record supplies context, while the compound evidence gives the guide its smaller scale.
Contextual Classic-period view anchored by existing urban record.

Burned architectural surfaces provide a different clock from pottery or inscriptions. At the Superimposed Buildings, archaeomagnetic measurements estimate the last strong heating experienced by sampled materials. Two models place it in the fifth century, while another yields an earlier range. Other sampled places produce still different or multiple possible dates. The city consequently should not change from flourishing to empty in one synchronized frame. This scene follows one measured burning context and keeps its chronological disagreement visible alongside the continuing urban landscape.
Last-heating estimates, not one proved city-wide destruction.

At La Ventilla, later burials cut through earlier walls and floors after buildings had fallen into disrepair. Burial 27 in LV 2 supplies a calibrated probability component of 540–610 CE, placing activity within a compound whose earlier organization had changed. The deposits show people engaging with an existing built environment rather than occupying a newly cleared blank space. LV 3 has a separate, later burial window. These observations support a local reuse sequence without making one neighborhood's history the timetable for the entire city.
Calibrated burial evidence; reoccupation inference.

sections.heading: Lives inside the old quarry landscape

paragraphs.text: The old quarry tunnels of Pirul and Varillas, behind the Sun Pyramid, became places of domestic, craft, burial and ritual activity. Their later occupants used spaces created by earlier extraction, adding another inhabited setting to the transformed city. The modeled Coyotlatelco phase spans approximately 640–820 CE. At this viewing year, the separately dated LV 3 burials also provide neighborhood evidence. Together the records reveal multiple places of activity after major political change, although they do not establish one unbroken citywide population or a single new community.
Modeled local occupation phase.

The tunnel sequence includes a Mazapa occupation phase modeled to 940–1230 CE. This takes the story well beyond the conventional endpoint of Teotihuacan's principal urban-development phase. The studied underground spaces preserve working and living activities, including evidence of bifacial tool production in Pirul. The workshop's precise position in every chronological phase is not independently established in this introductory report. The useful comparison is between a place's changing uses over centuries and the much shorter history of the government that built its great monuments.
Modeled local phase 940–1230 CE.

Aztec III occupation evidence returns the studied tunnel landscape to view in approximately 1390–1460 CE. The intervening local hiatus matters: later use is a new episode in an old place, not proof that every earlier neighborhood remained continuously occupied. Teotihuacan's monumental remains and excavated spaces continued to offer settings for activity long after the Classic city's political system had ended. This final scene closes with a layered landscape, allowing the later record to remain visible without extending the original urban government's lifetime.
Modeled evidence window after a local hiatus.

pages.title: Monte Albán
pages.intro: Explore a hilltop city’s household works, inscriptions, ballcourt and tomb reuse, with competing interpretations of government and conquest.

paragraphs.text: Around 500 BCE, Monte Albán's founders established a hilltop city whose residential terraces transformed a demanding setting. Households shared retaining walls and drainage arrangements, while farming and small-scale irrigation tied the settlement to surrounding land. Nicholas and Feinman use these material relationships to argue that coordinated production and comparatively collective institutions helped the city grow. Their argument redirects attention from a single ruler to the work needed to sustain neighborhoods. The approximate foundation date introduces this process rather than dating every terrace or irrigation feature.
Approximate foundation 500 BCE, encoded 1−500=-499.

The Danzantes carvings were not fixed forever in their first architectural setting. Winter argues that the original wall was dismantled after a relatively short period and that its stones entered later buildings. This reuse made earlier images available for new acts of remembrance. The figures themselves remain contested: a reading as remembered founding participants differs sharply from interpretations emphasizing captives and violence. The city-phase record anchors the viewing frame, while the wall's relative sequence provides a discussion of memory without inventing an exact demolition year.
Early urban era; relative sequence, not a dated demolition. The viewing year anchors the existing city phase, not the relative wall-reuse event.

sections.heading: Structure J and uncertain place names

paragraphs.text: Structure J incorporates carved monuments whose texts and images have often been read as a register of conquered places. Carter reassesses the proposed readings and the certainty of those identifications. The carvings are attributed to the Pe phase, approximately 300–100 BCE, but that estimate is not automatically the construction date of the entire building. Visitors can examine a specific material source for political claims while seeing why uncertain place names cannot safely become an imperial territory drawn on the map.
Pe-phase carving estimate 300–100 BCE; not automatically Structure J construction.

The ballcourt associated with the North Platform adds a named public structure to Monte Albán's monumental and residential landscape. INAH places its construction around 100 BCE. Its presence helps shift the narrative from the founding of a settlement to the repeated addition of spaces for public activity. The broad city record and the more specific ballcourt occurrence perform different jobs: one keeps the settlement in view, while the other marks a particular architectural intervention. Neither establishes a complete schedule for all surrounding plaza buildings.
Approximate construction 100 BCE.

The residence associated with Tomb 105 gives the Classic city a household and ancestral scale. Its existing construction record, approximately 500–800 CE, can be reused without creating a second version of the same claim. Mortuary space, residence and the wider terrace landscape belong in the same account of urban life. Connections with Teotihuacan are part of an earlier intercity history described by INAH, not evidence that all local political changes were imposed from outside. The scene places elite architecture beside the labor and food production sustaining the city.
Residence construction window 500–800; earlier contacts 200–500 are retrospective context.

Between roughly 800 and 900 CE, Monte Albán lost population and much of its earlier monumental prominence as the Oaxaca Valley's political geography changed. Feinman and Nicholas challenge the older picture of a simple Mixtec invasion replacing Zapotec society. A declining urban center and a reorganizing regional population are different historical processes. The existing city-phase record remains current here, while the guide explains decentralization as a transition in where people and institutions concentrated, without treating the end of major construction as the disappearance of all communities.
Approximate demographic/monumental change 800–900.

Tomb 7 combines an older burial structure with later Postclassic objects and activity. The broad 900–1520 CE interval describes that later assemblage and reuse, not the original construction of the tomb or a precisely dated single burial. This layered setting gives the final scene a different purpose from the earlier story of city growth. Localized Mixtec presence, particularly in later centuries, must be considered alongside continuing Zapotec communities. The site's ancestral significance could persist even as its former urban and political role changed.

pages.title: Calakmul
pages.intro: Follow a Maya centre through construction, murals, royal inscriptions and later use, separating political titles from the lives of the people around them.

sections.heading: An older monumental and hydraulic landscape

paragraphs.text: Structure II preserves sealed Preclassic deposits beneath the later monumental building. That sequence places Calakmul's history before the famous seventh-century Snake court. The surrounding landscape also includes seasonal bajos, reservoirs and canals, connecting urban life with the collection and management of water. Folan and colleagues describe these features at the scale of the settlement and its setting. They do not provide a construction year for every reservoir. The opening scene therefore introduces an established place and its environmental infrastructure without animating all components as one building campaign.
Illustrative view in existing Late Preclassic phase; no exact building construction year.

Chiik Nahb's Structure 1 was repeatedly rebuilt, preserving earlier versions inside later work. Carrasco Vargas and colleagues place the start of the construction sequence within approximately 420–620 CE. This building history makes a northern complex visible alongside the central monumental group. Its later murals and final remodeling belong to subsequent chapters, rather than being compressed into the date of its first construction. Following one structure through successive transformations gives the guide a concrete architectural thread that continues across changes in the city's court and political fortunes.
Ceramic-based start window 420–620 CE.

The monuments around Structure V establish a sequence of publicly displayed dates. Folan and colleagues identify northern stelae dated to 623 CE, while others around the structure belong to later seventh-century activity. Their positions connect political and ritual statements with movement through the central plaza. This is a narrower observation than saying the whole building was constructed in 623. The scene uses the dedication evidence to show monuments being added to an existing architectural setting, making the plaza a changing record of public memory.
Epigraphically dated dedication.

Stela 33, erected in 657, looks back to an accession in 579. That retrospective statement must not be mistaken for proof that the earlier king ruled from Calakmul. Martin distinguishes the Kaanu'l, or Snake, polity from the city itself and argues for its earlier seat at Dzibanche before a seventh-century transfer. The scene places the dated monument in Calakmul while allowing its text to refer elsewhere and earlier. Political identity, the location of a court and the age of a settlement consequently remain separate questions.
Stela 33 dedication in 657 anchors discussion of the broader seventh-century court transfer.

The murals of Structure 1, Sub 1–4, bring women, men, prepared foods and circulated goods into view. Their painted and written details include maize foods, salt and tobacco. A stylistic date of approximately 620–700 CE anchors this particular remodeling, rather than all activity in Chiik Nahb. The scenes broaden a history often dominated by kings and warfare by showing exchange and consumption. A market interpretation is plausible but debated; the paintings themselves do not establish a permanent market institution or the exact routes by which every commodity arrived.
Stylistic mural date 620–700 CE.

sections.heading: A defeat within continuing city life

paragraphs.text: INAH's historical account places Calakmul's defeat by Tikal in 695 CE. At that moment the existing broad urban-phase record remains current, and the mural phase also reaches into this period. A military setback therefore enters an already complex city history rather than replacing it with a simple abandonment event. The later construction sequence at Chiik Nahb supplies an important comparison in the next scene. Changes in royal power, the ability to commission monuments and the everyday continuation of local activity need separate evidence and separate dates.
Military event in institutional synthesis; not a destruction date. Existing urban-phase record provides current city context; no independently added military-event record.

The final remodeling of Chiik Nahb's Structure 1 began within the broad 820–1020 CE interval and was left unfinished. This material sequence extends well beyond the old record's selected major-urban-phase endpoint of 700. INAH also reports a last dated stela in 909, a different category of evidence from construction stratigraphy. The two observations help keep late activity visible while resisting a false exact ending. An unfinished project can reveal disrupted work, but it does not identify the last inhabitant or by itself explain why the project stopped.
Final-remodeling initiation window 820–1020 CE.

sections.heading: Visits to an older sacred city

paragraphs.text: INAH recounts that Alonso de Ávila encountered the old city in the early sixteenth century and observed occasional Indigenous ritual visits. The underlying colonial text was not verified in this pass, so the record remains an attributed documentary account with a coarse first-half-century window. Its historical subject is visitation to an older sacred place, not the continuation of the Classic court. This later layer allows the guide to end with remembered and reused spaces, while keeping the observed activity distinct from both dense urban occupation and twentieth-century archaeological work.

pages.title: Copán
pages.intro: Explore buried architectural phases, Oropéndola and the Hieroglyphic Stairway, then the evidence for activity after royal monumental production changed.

paragraphs.text: Excavation beneath the Northern Court Complex reaches constructions assigned to approximately 350–400 CE, before the royal Acropolis took its later form. Investigators reached these levels below the later buildings around Court 4 B, including Loro, Tucán and Pato. Their names locate the excavated context but do not give those later buildings the dates of the deposits beneath them. The opening scene establishes a place already being built and used, allowing the subsequent appearance of royal architecture to be understood as a transformation of an earlier landscape.
Viewing year within report's approximate Division VI, 350–400 CE.

Within the early Acropolis sequence, Hunal stands out for its red-painted talud-tablero façade and north-facing stair. Nearby Tartan marked a boundary between an early ballcourt complex and the Acropolis, while other buildings and drains expanded the constructed setting. These features belong to the report's broad 400–450 CE division. Hunal's architectural form invites comparison with central Mexico, but resemblance alone cannot demonstrate conquest or a person's ethnicity. The building and associated tomb support investigation of dynastic beginnings while leaving their more specific identifications open to additional evidence.
Viewing frame within Division V, 400–450 CE; not exact Hunal construction or founder accession.

Oropéndola survives inside Structure 10 L-16, making the later pyramid a container for earlier architectural histories. Its carved stone mosaic façade differs from the modeled stucco associated with other early buildings, and its arrangement can be compared with nearby Rosalila. Stratigraphy suggests construction around 550–600 CE; lintel samples and ceramics provide additional checks. The Spanish dating section and full context resolve an erroneous BCE label in the English abstract. This scene follows a particular temple's construction rather than assigning the same age to every buried building in the Acropolis.
Viewing year within suggested construction window 550–600 CE.

In 710 CE, according to Fash's research account, Ruler 13 dedicated the first Hieroglyphic Stairway to commemorate Ruler 12, who had died in 695. The inscription and architectural sequence connect a public stairway with a royal burial and remembered reign. Archaeological investigation beneath the structure supports the distinction between this first version and its later extension. The stairs thus record an act of making history visible in stone, while the current date belongs to the dedication rather than to every event recalled in its text.
Epigraphic dedication year in Fash's 2017 research account.

The expanded Hieroglyphic Stairway received another dedication under Ruler 15, dated to 755 CE in Fash's account. Different carving styles help distinguish the earlier and later inscriptions, even though fallen and rearranged blocks complicate their reconstruction. References to Ruler 13's death at the hands of Quiriguá place conflict within the monument's political story. The renewed building effort also demonstrates that defeat did not simply stop dynastic representation. A one-year difference in some institutional summaries is retained as a chronological discrepancy rather than silently resolved.
Later dedication year in Fash's 2017 account; one-year variants occur in institutional summaries.

sections.heading: Households, rainwater and a changing court

paragraphs.text: Copán's residents relied on water collection and distribution as well as the royal monuments that dominate surviving views. Research interprets the East, West and Hieroglyphic Stairway courts as parts of a rainwater-collection system, and investigation near Las Sepulturas supports an ancient pond. Índigo and Temple 22 connect drainage and water imagery; Structure 9 N-82 brings maize and water symbolism into a residential setting. These features link subsistence, community organization and authority, although their exact operating dates and the proposed social relationships are not all independently established.
Illustrative late Classic viewing year, supported by existing broad phase and the later-activity model; water features lack independent narrow dates here.

An influential 1990 settlement model separates the decline of royal authority around 800 CE from continuing nonroyal elite activity over roughly two more centuries. Its evidence came from a large program of survey, excavation and obsidian-hydration dating. This makes the wider settlement landscape central to the question of what followed the royal court. The result remains an older, method-dependent model, accessed here through its abstracts. It supports a carefully labeled later-activity scene rather than a claim that a particular palace was still occupied in 950.
Viewing year within an older model of subroyal activity, approximately 800–1000 CE; confidence explicitly limited.

pages.title: Paquimé
pages.intro: Follow earlier houses, the multistorey town, animal husbandry and a directly dated interment. Wider connections did not make this place a copy of another city.

paragraphs.text: INAH's account begins with pit-house settlements near streams and springs around 600 CE, well before the surviving multistory town. Their setting puts access to water and everyday settlement choices at the beginning of the story. Around 900, the institutional sequence describes a change toward earthen courtyard houses. The early interval is a broad place-area phase, not a direct date for the later public buildings. Keeping it separate makes Paquimé's development visible without projecting its eventual monumental form backward over several centuries.
Illustrative frame within official early-settlement account, approximately 600–900 CE.

Around 900 CE, the official sequence describes a transition from pit houses to earthen-walled houses arranged around courtyards. Household and workshop spaces provide a view of architecture organized around recurring activities rather than isolated monuments. The approximate date marks a change in the settlement account; it is not evidence that every household rebuilt at once. Later mitochondrial research also challenges a simple population-replacement explanation for Paquimé's growth, although those maternal-line results cannot assign identities or origins to the occupants of any particular courtyard.
Approximate change around 900 CE; not an exactly dated citywide rebuilding.

During the Medio period, large residential units, plazas, specialized buildings and public works transformed Paquimé's scale. Casa Amurallada is a named component that INAH assigns to this phase, while the existing town record supplies the conventional 1200–1450 CE frame. Some regional chronologies begin the phase closer to 1150, so the starting boundary remains approximate. Recent mitochondrial results suggest substantial maternal-line continuity across the town's rise. Architectural elaboration and increasing connections therefore need not be narrated as a new population simply replacing an older one.
Viewing year near conventional Medio onset; regional chronology can start around 1150 or 1200.

The water system connected collection, filtering, storage and distribution with life inside the town. INAH describes the Depósito de Agua, a principal reservoir and channels supplying residential spaces. These components help explain the maintenance and coordination needed to sustain dense earthen architecture. Irrigation also belongs to the wider agricultural account, but it should not be confused with a fully reconstructed street-by-street supply network. The viewing year falls within the town's broad phase; no independent narrow construction date was verified for each tank, filter or channel.
Illustrative view within the broad town phase; no independently dated construction year for each channel.

Scarlet macaws connect Paquimé's architecture with animal care, specialized labor and wider circulation. Casa de las Guacamayas provides a named setting for bird keeping, while isotope research on 29 specimens indicates that most were probably raised locally, with some possible nonlocal origins. The checked abstract does not establish that every sampled bird came from that house. Nor do strontium values trace a unique trade route. The scene therefore brings local husbandry into the exchange story rather than treating every exotic bird as a newly imported object.
Illustrative Medio-phase frame; isotope specimens are not independently assigned to 1320.

sections.heading: A dated act at the House of the Well

paragraphs.text: The House of the Well contains an activity dated more directly than many of the town's architectural phases: an interment associated with its central roof-support post. The radiocarbon result calibrates to 1301–1397 CE at 95.4% probability. Tree-ring measurements from the building are older and lack outer rings, preventing their simple use as exact construction dates. The source interprets the interment in relation to ritual and the building's erection. Those interpretations remain distinct from the measured dating result and from claims about the entire community.
Viewing frame within calibrated 1301–1397 CE, 95.4% probability.

By the fifteenth century, Paquimé's large-scale occupation declined, closing the main phase represented in the existing town record. The conventional 1450 boundary organizes a body of archaeological evidence; it does not identify one last resident or prove that every building ended simultaneously. The earlier scenes show why such a distinction matters: households, water systems, bird keeping and ritual activities each have their own records. The result was a transformed regional landscape. Specific causes, later connections and the histories of living communities require their own evidence; the end of this building phase does not establish their disappearance.
Late-phase viewing frame; approximately fifteenth-century decline, not a last-person date.

pages.title: Poverty Point
pages.intro: Explore individually dated earthworks and habitation, and the materials connecting Poverty Point with a wider world.

paragraphs.text: Six concentric ridge segments and an open central area organized a complex that also included substantial mounds. Mound A has a western cone, an eastern platform and a ramp, with different sediments and construction treatments. Its form should not be reduced to the popular but unproven claim that it was deliberately a bird effigy. Timber-circle traces reveal another architectural medium: wood could mark gathering spaces even when no standing posts survive.

The 2024 chronology argues for relatively concentrated building. Dates below a mound are older than its construction; they do not directly date its completed surface. That distinction matters when comparing mound construction, plaza filling and use of the ridges.

paragraphs.text: Wetland foods and upland resources supported a substantial settled community. Archaeological syntheses identify fish and other aquatic animals, aquatic plants, nuts, fruits and seeds. Heated clay objects substituted for scarce local cooking stones and could be used in earth ovens. Their abundance reflects repeated food preparation rather than evidence that farming was required to organize monument building.

Imported material was not reserved for one narrow category of prestige object. Tool making, cooking vessels and ornament drew on varied rocks and minerals. Copper provenance is a question about compositional similarity to sampled geological sources, with uncertainty remaining over precise sources and the mechanisms of movement. Neither a chemical group nor a distant source establishes the path taken by an artifact.

sections.heading: Three clocks that should stay distinct

paragraphs.text: The existing institutional settlement interval, 1700–1100 BCE, is a broad synthesis. Kidder and Grooms instead model a selected sequence, with start-boundary uncertainty at 3535–3430 cal BP and end-boundary uncertainty at 3250–3135 cal BP, both at 95.4% probability. Their approximate 3300–3200 cal BP construction pulse is a third kind of claim. None of these is a dated census of continuous occupation.

Calibrated BP uses 1950 as its reference year. The numbers in the model can therefore be placed on a calendar after calibration; a raw radiocarbon measurement cannot be converted by simply subtracting it from 1950. Earlier dates from residual or naturally burned material need not mark cultural activity or the founding of a mound.

Poverty Point belongs in comparisons of community organization and monument building, but similarity to another earthwork landscape does not establish ancestry or direct transmission. Its relationship with earlier Lower Mississippi Valley sites is a chronological research question, not proof that one center invented an entire regional culture.

Labor arrangements, the social obligations behind imported materials and the meaning of repeated timber structures remain open. The evidence supports skill, planning and sustained connections while leaving considerable uncertainty about leadership and ritual. Those limits are more informative than assigning an undocumented king, migration or catastrophic ending.

pages.title: Hopewell earthworks
pages.intro: Visit distinct earthwork complexes and compare their chronologies, ceremonial spaces and material connections without making them one city.

paragraphs.text: Mound City, Hopewell Mound Group and Seip occupy different places and preserve different combinations of buildings, earthworks and deposits. Mound City has a compact enclosure with numerous mounds; Hopewell Mound Group joins a D-shaped enclosure and square; Seip combines circles, a square and substantial submound architecture. The public locators identify each complex, not individual graves or households.

rows.name: Mound City
rows.dates: Existing broad phase 1–400 CE
rows.architecture: Enclosure, mounds, buildings and prepared ceremonial facilities.
rows.limits: Reconstructed surfaces and broad phase dates do not date every structure.

rows.name: Hopewell Mound Group
rows.dates: Modeled start 150–205; end 365–420 CE (68.3%)
rows.architecture: D-shaped and square enclosures, submound buildings and activity areas.
rows.limits: Separate probability ranges, not one occupation interval.

rows.name: Seip
rows.dates: Modeled start 170–295; end 355–500 CE (68.3%)
rows.architecture: Circular/square geometry, Seip-Pricer and additional buildings.
rows.limits: Seven selected dates; present central mound is reconstructed.

paragraphs.text: Ohio Hopewell contexts include shaped copper, stone tools and ornaments, effigy pipes and other carefully worked materials. Their placement in buildings, basins or offerings matters as much as their appearance. A center could be a place of production and gathering without resembling a densely occupied urban neighborhood. The distribution of activities around monuments complicates simple images of empty ritual sites or ordinary residential towns.

At Seip, connected building remains, fire features and the burned offering provide specific settings for interpreting objects. Deliberate burning should first be understood in those settings; it cannot be treated as evidence of a shared regional calamity merely because other centers also contain burned materials.

The 2023 study evaluated a large radiocarbon corpus and compared increasingly selective sets. Its main regional onset is not simply 90–120 CE: that interval holds only 36.2% of probability, with another 32.1% at 130–170 CE. The broader 95.4% onset range is 70–185 CE. Reporting just the first interval would conceal the second probability peak.

Individual-center models give different boundaries. Charcoal, annual plant material and artifacts can have different relationships to the activities being dated. Long-lived wood, residual deposits and mixed contexts are among the reasons that chronological selection matters. A model boundary is a statistical estimate for a chosen sequence, not an observed year when all ceremonies began or ended.

Barnes and Lepper’s drum proposal is a concrete example of interpretation shaped by Indigenous knowledge. Comparison with Shawnee drum construction gives the Seip spheres a possible functional context that earlier labels missed. The proposal remains testable and uncertain; acknowledging that uncertainty does not diminish the contribution of the knowledge that generated it.

Hopewell is an archaeological term covering related practices, materials and ceremonial landscapes. It is not a demonstrated single language, tribe or centralized state. Archaeology can trace changes in those practices without claiming that Indigenous peoples vanished when a material style changed. The named complexes invite comparison with other earthwork traditions while retaining their separate local histories.

pages.title: San Agustín
pages.intro: Follow local settlements, burial architecture and sculpture through their separate histories in the upper Magdalena.

paragraphs.text: Mesita A, B and C are neighboring archaeological groups rather than interchangeable names for one monument. A has two principal funerary mounds; B combines three large mounds with a long residential and ceremonial history; C has a smaller funerary arrangement and a reported seventh-century context. Their relationships are best understood through buildings, deposits and household distributions together.

rows.name: Mesita A
rows.dates: Regional Classic, 1–900 CE
rows.architecture: Principal mounds with corridors, chambers and statues; simpler surrounding tombs.
rows.limits: A broad cultural attribution does not date each burial.

rows.name: Mesita B and Household 68
rows.dates: Formative residential history; Regional Classic monuments
rows.architecture: Mounds, statues and differentiated household/craft evidence.
rows.limits: Public Mesitas locator is not a household coordinate; social rank is interpreted.

rows.name: Mesita C
rows.dates: Seventh-century CE funerary summary
rows.architecture: Former mound, statues and numerous simpler tombs.
rows.limits: Assays and calibration probabilities absent from the checked guide; earlier disturbance matters.

rows.name: La Estación
rows.dates: Recent, 900–1350 CE in this guide
rows.architecture: Approximately 9 m structure, interpreted as ceremonial.
rows.limits: Function and exact building position remain less secure than the phase-associated structure itself.

paragraphs.text: The Mesitas research combines extensive shovel probing with artifact distributions to identify household clusters. Its ceramic phases provide broad comparisons through time, not year-by-year population totals. Household 68’s unusual pottery density is evidence of a distinctive activity area, but identifying feasts, collective storage or other specific activities requires more than a dense scatter alone.

During the Regional Classic, different parts of the core show contrasting relationships with gold ornament production, pottery making, obsidian exchange and ritual. González interprets this as several sources of influence and possible competition among prominent groups. The material distinctions are firmer than a reconstruction of tribute obligations, kinship factions or named offices.

sections.heading: Stone figures and the treatment of the dead

paragraphs.text: The best-known sculptures were parts of funerary architecture and inhabited landscapes. Monumental chambers and simpler surrounding tombs expressed differences in treatment after death. Rich sculpture does not necessarily imply abundant grave goods, and variation between neighboring groups should not be flattened into one standard ceremony.

A and B preserve stronger archaeological context for reconstructing some arrangements than areas disturbed before systematic study. The carved streambed at Fuente de Lavapatas has a broad stylistic attribution, but the checked sources do not provide a sufficiently secure construction date for a separate timed movie chapter. Its channels and figures can be discussed without manufacturing an exact building year.

The park guide uses Formative 1 at 1000–600 BCE, Formative 2 at 600–300 BCE, Formative 3 at 300 BCE–1 CE, Regional Classic at 1–900 CE, and Recent at 900–1350 CE. These are archaeological conventions, with other regional works extending Recent to 1530. They should not be stitched into exact occupation endpoints or a single uninterrupted political history.

After the principal statuary-and-tomb tradition, ceramic change, agricultural intensification and the La Estación building suggest altered ways of organizing work and ceremony. The evidence does not securely assign all phases to one named language or a modern ethnic identity. Comparison with Tierradentro is useful for architecture and settlement, provided local chronologies and social histories remain distinct.

pages.title: Tierradentro
pages.intro: Explore named tomb groups alongside settlement evidence, distinguishing uncertain tomb dates from better-resolved local occupation phases.

paragraphs.text: The public archaeological groups preserve different choices in chamber size, roof treatment, supports and decoration. Segovia includes elaborate carved pillars and painted interiors; El Duende D4 has a rectangular room and distinctive roof form; El Aguacate generally has smaller chambers without central columns. These differences deserve comparison without automatically turning them into separate peoples or a precise developmental sequence.

rows.name: Alto de Segovia
rows.dates: Conventional hypogeum window approximately 600–900 CE, contested
rows.architecture: Named chambers S1, S4 and S9; pillars, niches and painting.
rows.limits: Direct chamber construction dates are not established by the guide.

rows.name: El Duende
rows.dates: Same provisional tradition attribution
rows.architecture: D4 rectangular chamber, roof treatment and geometric painting.
rows.limits: Architectural variation is not itself an absolute date.

rows.name: El Aguacate
rows.dates: Same provisional tradition attribution
rows.architecture: Small ridge-top chambers; A0 with distinctive painted motifs.
rows.limits: Domestic layer near A60 has no precise date in this source check.

rows.name: El Tablón
rows.dates: Middle settlement context 100–1300 CE
rows.architecture: Anthropomorphic statuary, often with pectorals.
rows.limits: Settlement phase does not directly date carving of individual stones.

sections.heading: Burial practices and the houses of the living

paragraphs.text: Hypogea could receive human remains after initial burial elsewhere, so a bone’s biological age and its later deposition are different events. Carved architectural forms and painted interiors made the chambers more than storage spaces, but the sources do not preserve a complete account of ceremonies or the identities of participants.

Regional survey places the monuments among changing settlements. Early 3 concentrations at Segovia, Middle-period occupation around El Tablón and later residence near San Andrés prevent the funerary landscape from being treated as isolated from daily life. The domestic layer at El Aguacate is especially useful as a warning against assuming that all tomb groups stood apart from habitation.

sections.heading: Two chronological systems and a translation error

paragraphs.text: The regional study uses Early 3 at 300 BCE–100 CE, Middle at 100–1300 CE and Late at 1300–1650 CE. These local ceramic phases differ from the generalized Alto Magdalena sequence. Their boundaries should not be exchanged merely because period names appear similar.

The English park guide prints 600–900 BC for the hypogea where the Spanish version reads 600–900 d.C. The CE reading is used here, with the uncertainty emphasized in the sources. The regional study also reports contamination problems with extremely early apparent bone dates. Neither the mistranslation nor contaminated samples justify a new early tomb-building episode.

The archaeological park lies within the Nasa resguardo of San Andrés. That present relationship is essential context for understanding the place, while the checked archaeological sources do not establish a single language or an unbroken named identity for every ancient monument builder. Historical accounts themselves describe several peoples and uncertain territorial limits.

Tierradentro and San Agustín share useful points of comparison in statuary, mortuary architecture and the relationship between monuments and settlement. Their local sequences should nevertheless remain separate. More secure dating, contextual research and Indigenous knowledge can refine those relationships without requiring the current gaps to be filled by an invented migration or common political state.

pages.title: Casarabe urban landscapes
pages.intro: Look at individual centers and engineered landscapes, separating dated construction, regional models and later agricultural evidence.

paragraphs.text: Cotoca and Landívar are major centers, while Cerrito, Santa María and Salvatierra show other scales and configurations of the same broad architectural tradition. Lidar identifies elevated platforms, enclosures and connections; excavation at Salvatierra supplies stratigraphy and dated samples. Combining these approaches reveals a connected landscape without making every mapped structure contemporary.

rows.name: Cotoca
rows.dates: Regional association approximately 500–1400 CE
rows.architecture: Large raised core, U-shaped and other platforms, multiple enclosures and causeways.
rows.limits: No directly dated sequence for every enclosure; approximately 147 ha is enclosed area.

rows.name: Landívar
rows.dates: Regional association approximately 500–1400 CE
rows.architecture: Platforms beside a former channel, three enclosing circuits and raised approaches.
rows.limits: 315 ha outer enclosure does not measure dense housing or population.

rows.name: Cerrito
rows.dates: Regional association approximately 500–1400 CE
rows.architecture: Raised platform core, substantial structures, enclosure and connected causeways.
rows.limits: Individual construction phases remain undated in this source.

rows.name: Santa María
rows.dates: Regional association approximately 500–1400 CE
rows.architecture: Platforms, dams, reservoirs and enclosing earthwork.
rows.limits: Do not confuse its reservoirs with Pond 690 in the separate farming study.

rows.name: Salvatierra
rows.dates: Selected Phase 1 sample 495–591; Phase 5 sample 1081–1158 CE, modeled 95.4%
rows.architecture: Excavated deposits within an architectural complex with platforms and water storage.
rows.limits: Sample dates do not individually date all buildings or demonstrate uninterrupted occupation.

paragraphs.text: Water could be both an excess and a scarce resource. Canals could drain savannah soils in wet months, while reservoirs and farm ponds retained water through drier periods. Santa María’s arrangements provide a named architectural example of water management; the separately sampled agricultural ponds address a different scale of evidence. The purposes of every canal and basin should not be treated as identical.

The 2025 study examined 178 phytolith samples from eighteen profiles. Maize dominates the sampled agricultural evidence, but the body of the paper also reports Cucurbita in two adjacent pond samples and a Manihot pollen grain. The proposed seasonal farming system and possibility of multiple harvests do not establish that all regional food consumption was maize, nor that every household followed one uniform strategy.

Causeways connect some known centers and branch through an engineered landscape. Gaps and platforms near enclosure crossings have been interpreted as restricted access, while some enclosure forms may have had defensive roles. These are functional hypotheses from architecture, not documentation of named wars, armies or boundaries. Other causeways have no identified destination, leaving their daily or ceremonial uses unresolved.

The study proposes a settlement hierarchy with several tiers and describes low-density urbanism: monumental centers embedded within a broad modified landscape. That interpretation does not supply a precise population or prove one centralized state. Smaller unmounded settlements may be less visible in lidar, so the mapped hierarchy is also shaped by what the method can detect.

The regional 500–1400 CE horizon comes from dated excavations and archaeological comparisons. At Salvatierra, the selected Phase 1 and Phase 5 contexts are modeled charcoal likelihoods within a stratigraphic sequence. A charcoal age is not automatically the date when a platform was raised, and early samples beneath buildings can represent natural activity or earlier use rather than the Casarabe construction itself.

Pond 690’s approximately 1250–1550 calendar CE sequence was modeled from sediment dates. It extends later than the broad urban-system horizon and is retained as its own observation. The result cannot extend the occupation of every town to 1550 or establish the cultural identity of every later pond user. Sampled forest profiles likewise leave other woodland uses possible even where cultivation and fire were not detected.

pages.title: Nan Madol: building, water and chiefly life
pages.intro: Follow separate construction projects in Nan Madol and the evidence for changing use; an early tomb date is not the beginning of every islet.

paragraphs.text: Nan Madol combines monumental basalt architecture with coral deposits used in construction. Dates from an enclosing wall and central-vault fill at Nandowas should remain separate observations, even when both contribute to one tomb complex’s history.

Relative sea-level reconstruction indicates that the site’s construction-era water setting differed from its modern appearance. Present canals and shorelines cannot simply be projected backward unchanged. This environmental result does not erase human engineering.

The 2024 coral chronology distinguishes an early phase, a concentrated early cluster and a larger later phase. Climatic or political explanations are interpretations of those patterns; the ages do not by themselves prove a universal crisis, forced-labor system or exact date of political replacement.

The nomination’s historical discussion and the World Heritage description connect Nan Madol to continuing chiefly authority and social practice. The archaeological study concerns a living cultural inheritance, rather than an unnamed vanished population.

The nomination is internally uneven: its summary ends residential use by the 1820s, while its detailed history retains chiefly occupation on a few islets into the early 1900s. Its 1826–1885 phase supplies a context window, not a dated assembly or continuous occupation of every islet. Ceremonial significance and household residence are separate.

pages.title: Budj Bim: an engineered water landscape
pages.intro: Explore engineering and settlement in the Budj Bim cultural landscape with distinct dates for landforms, construction and continued use.

sections.heading: Country provides the setting; engineering has its own chronology

paragraphs.text: Budj Bim’s lava landscape gave later communities a particular terrain of rock and water. The eruption, the earliest dated channel infill and later wall building are different events. None should be used as a substitute date for the others.

sections.heading: Reading a system rather than an isolated wall

paragraphs.text: Channels, weirs and dams worked together with wetlands to manage and harvest aquatic resources, including kooyang, short-finned eels. Excavation at Muldoons identifies successive local construction episodes; the whole landscape cannot be assigned one uniform building year.

The World Heritage property comprises a northern component around Tae Rak, central Kurtonitj and southern Tyrendarra. The public component coordinates orient the reader within a large cultural landscape. They do not identify individual channels, private places or excavation grids.

sections.heading: Residence, access and the companion community history

paragraphs.text: The Kurtonitj house and Lake Condah Mission add nineteenth-century histories to the engineering record. They have their own dates and meanings. Gunditjmara histories follows the people and colonial institutions; this place study follows how evidence is situated in the landscape.

pages.title: Gunditjmara histories: Country, work and persistence
pages.intro: Connect engineered Country with Gunditjmara community histories, colonial intrusion, coercive institutions and continuing agency.

sections.heading: A living people, not an extinct archaeological category

paragraphs.text: Gunditjmara community institutions describe continuing responsibilities to Country. Archaeological records add dated observations to that history without setting its beginning or its end. The pre-1935 display limit is an atlas boundary, not a statement about survival.

The Muldoons sequence documents local engineering changes, while Kurtonitj documents a household context centuries later. Neither assemblage stands for every Gunditjmara person. Their different dates and methods are preserved so that community history is not compressed into one material style.

Lake Condah Mission followed resistance to removal from Country. Colonial supervision and the 1886 exclusionary policy then constrained residence. Describing those constraints also requires retaining community choices, family connections and the continuing importance of the site.

sections.heading: How this study connects to Budj Bim

paragraphs.text: Budj Bim owns the detailed aquaculture observations and the landscape chronology. This guide owns the Kurtonitj household and mission-history observations. Shared chapter links make the connection explicit without duplicating the underlying events.

pages.title: Lapita communities and successors
pages.intro: Follow particular settlements and connections across islands, then ask what changed after the archaeological label Lapita ceased to describe pottery.

sections.heading: What the name Lapita can and cannot do

paragraphs.text: Lapita is an archaeological category built around material patterns, especially decorated pottery. It is useful for comparing sites, but it is not a single ethnic identity, a biological ancestry or a language automatically readable from a potsherd.

Kamgot’s shoreline reconstruction and plant and marine remains bring local work into a history often dominated by voyaging. Uripiv’s isotope study adds evidence about diet and childhood residence. These methods answer different questions and must retain their own limits.

Fishing assemblages, exchanged materials and related material practices demonstrate maritime connections at different scales. They do not authorize drawing a particular family’s voyage between every sampled site. Chronological models can compare island sequences while leaving uncertain routes uncertain.

sections.heading: After decorated pottery, and among living communities

paragraphs.text: Later occupation at Uripiv shows why the end of a pottery category is not an automatic departure. Vanuatu Cultural Centre authors also describe the contemporary significance of Lapita research. That living engagement is acknowledged here without adding post-1934 events to the historical map.
